question: Isn't it arrogant to say that Jesus is the only way to God, and that billions of sincere believers in other faiths are wrong?

ledger.heading: Twentieth run (2026-11-20): an independent editor's read of the morality area, and the area "Other religions, and those who never heard"

shortAnswer: It can be said arrogantly, and Christians have often said it that way, with contempt and sometimes with an empire behind them. That is sin, and it should be named. But the claim itself is not arrogant, for two reasons. Every view of the religions excludes others, the pluralist's included: to say that no faith has the whole truth is to tell every believer that his faith is mistaken about what matters most to him. And the Christian claim, read where it first stands, is not a boast. Jesus said "I am the way" to a frightened friend on the night before he died, and Peter said there is "no other name" as a prisoner on trial. What they claimed is that salvation is a gift in a person, which no one earns and no one is born into. Whether that is true is the real question.

sections.heading: The objection at its strongest
sections.body:
The objection is first of all moral, and it comes from people who have thought hard about the religions. Wilfred Cantwell Smith wrote in 1976, as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's article on religious diversity quotes him, that "except at the cost of insensitivity or delinquency, it is morally not possible actually to go out into the world and say to devout, intelligent fellow human beings [that] we believe that we know God and we are right; you believe that you know God, and you are totally wrong." The philosopher John Hick, in *An Interpretation of Religion* (1989), held that those who claim their faith alone is true often show a kind of arbitrariness or arrogance, and the philosopher Joseph Runzo judged such exclusivism presumptuous and morally objectionable, as the same article reports their views.

At full strength the objection says this. Most of the people who have ever lived were not Christians. Many of them were wiser and kinder than many Christians. They prayed, gave to the poor, forgave their enemies and died well. To say that all of them were wrong about God, and that Christians alone have the truth, is to set yourself above most of the human race on a matter no one can prove. And the claim has a history. It was carried by armies and colonizers, used to justify conquest and forced conversion, and spoken in a tone that treated other peoples' holiest things as rubbish. A claim that has been used so, and that requires one to think so little of so many, should be given up.

sections.heading: What is true in it
sections.body:
The history is true, and no Christian should soften it. The claim that Jesus is the only way has been spoken from thrones and carried on the decks of ships of conquest, and people have been baptized under threat. The site's pages on the church's record name some of that history, and they name it as the church's own sin.

It is also true that many Christians say this with no idea what they're denying. They speak of Islam without having read the Qur'an, of Judaism without knowing what a Jewish neighbor prays on a Sabbath evening, of Hinduism and Buddhism as if they were one thing. Holding a conviction while knowing nothing of what others hold is not faithfulness. It is laziness, and it makes the claim sound like what the objection says it is.

And the objection is right that the claim cuts close. To tell a devout person that his faith is mistaken about God is not a small thing. Christians who say it lightly have not understood what they are saying. The New Testament itself tells Christians to give their reasons "with gentleness and respect" (1 Peter 3:15, BSB), and when two of Jesus' own disciples wanted fire on a village that would not receive him, "Jesus turned and rebuked them" (Luke 9:55, BSB).

sections.heading: The evidence
sections.body:
Begin with the words themselves, where they stand. "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me" (John 14:6, BSB) was not a slogan shouted at rival religions. It was an answer to Thomas, who had just said, "we do not know where You are going, so how can we know the way?" (John 14:5, BSB). It was the night Jesus was betrayed, and his friends were afraid. He didn't give Thomas a method or a school of thought. He gave himself. The Study Bible's note on John 14 puts it this way: Jesus "does not say he knows the way or teaches the way, but that he is the way."

The second text is Peter's: "Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4:12, BSB). Peter and John had been arrested after a lame man was healed, and they stood before the council that had handed Jesus over. The council saw "that they were unschooled, ordinary men" (Acts 4:13, BSB). The Study Bible's note on Acts 4 makes the point the objection misses: "Peter is not a powerful man imposing his religion on the weak; he is a prisoner on trial before the powerful." The claim was born without power, and its first speakers paid for it.

Then look at what the claim says. It says that salvation is in a person, not in a people, a ritual, a philosophy or a level of moral achievement. Paul draws the consequence himself: "it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9, BSB). If the claim is true, then Christians are not saved because they were born in the right place or worked out the right answer. They are beggars who have been fed. A Christian who boasts about it has not understood it.

Notice, too, whom the claim includes. It belongs to no nation and no culture. Paul told the Athenians that God "made every nation of men" from one man (Acts 17:26, BSB), and John's vision of the end is of "a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb" (Revelation 7:9, BSB). The one way is the same way for a fisherman in Galilee, a philosopher in Athens and a Roman officer in Caesarea, and it was offered to all of them on the same terms. A claim that ranked peoples or cultures would be arrogant. This one ranks none of them.

Finally, look at the other views. The pluralist holds that no religion knows the ultimate as it is and that all the great faiths are equally paths to it. That view, too, is denied by the central teaching of each great tradition as its own believers hold it, and it can't be proved. As the Stanford Encyclopedia sets out the reply that the philosopher Alvin Plantinga and others have made, exclusivists deny that it is arrogant to hold and to share a belief one has good reason to think true, especially when one believes it matters for the good of those one shares it with. If believing something most people deny is arrogant, then nearly everyone who holds a view about religion is arrogant, and the charge tells us nothing about which view is true.

sections.heading: The argument, laid out
sections.intro: This is an argument that the charge of arrogance doesn't settle the question, and that the Christian claim, rightly held, is not arrogant in itself.
steps: Every account of the religions, pluralism and secular unbelief included, holds that many sincere people are mistaken about the most important things they believe, so holding a view that excludes others can't by itself be arrogant.
Arrogance is a matter of how a belief is held and carried: in contempt for others, without knowing them, or with the use of power to compel them.
The Christian claim, as its texts state it, places salvation in a gift no one earns, forbids boasting, and commands that it be offered with gentleness and respect and never by force.
sections.conclusion: So: the charge of arrogance falls on Christians who have held or carried the claim in contempt or by force, and that is the church's sin; it doesn't fall on the claim itself, and the question that remains is whether the claim is true.
sections.after: The weight sits on the first step. The objection's best reply is that exclusivism is not like other views, because it says other people are wrong about God, which is worse than being wrong about philosophy. That reply is weighed next.

sections.heading: The strongest reply, and an answer
sections.body:
The strongest reply is Smith's: there is something different about telling a devout, intelligent person that he is "totally wrong" about God. A philosophical disagreement is one thing. To tell a grandmother who has prayed faithfully for sixty years that her prayers went to no one, or that she is lost, is cruelty, whatever the logic.

Part of this has to be granted. The Christian claim does have consequences that a Christian should feel, and a Christian who doesn't feel them hasn't understood it. But the reply runs two things together. The Christian claim is about who saves: that whoever is saved is saved by Christ. It isn't a claim to know the end of any person, and Christians disagree about how God deals with those who never heard of Christ or never heard of him rightly, as this library's page on that question sets out. Nor does the Christian claim say that the grandmother's prayers met no one. Paul told the Athenians that God "is not far from each one of us" (Acts 17:27, BSB).

And the pluralist's own view is not gentler at this point. It tells the Muslim grandmother that the Qur'an she recites is not literally true, and the Christian that Jesus was not raised as an event. Every serious view of the religions tells some devout person that he is wrong. The only honest choice is between saying so with respect, having first understood what he believes, and saying so with contempt. Smith himself was right that the second is wicked. Respect for a person includes taking his claims seriously enough to say where one disagrees.

That leaves the question the charge of arrogance had covered over: is it true? The Christian answer rests on an event, that Jesus was raised from the dead, and Paul said that if it didn't happen the faith is "futile" (1 Corinthians 15:17, BSB). That can be weighed, and the library's pages on the resurrection weigh it.

sections.heading: What remains unresolved
sections.body: How a Christian should speak about Christ among friends and family of other faiths, so that the claim is neither hidden nor used as a weapon, is learned in practice more than settled in argument. What the claim means for those who never heard is taken up on its own page. And whether the resurrection happened is a historical question this page leaves to the pages that argue it.

sections.heading: Where Christians differ
sections.body: Christians differ on how God's saving work in Christ reaches people: some hold that a person must hear the gospel and believe in this life, others that Christ may save some who never knew his name, and a few hope that all will finally be saved. They differ on how to share their faith with people of other faiths, and on what part dialogue between religions should play. What all confess together is that salvation is in Christ alone and is a gift of grace, that God "wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:4, BSB), and that no one may be forced or shamed into faith.
